chunks: Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ismāʿīl ibn Marrār, from Yūnus, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said:

I asked him about a man who had offered a sacrificial animal and it became broken. He said: If it was guaranteed, and the guaranteed one is that which was due because of an oath—meaning a vow or an expiation—then its compensation is upon him. I said: May he eat from it? He said: No; it is only for the needy. But if it was not guaranteed, then nothing is upon him. I said: May he eat from it? He said: He may eat from it.

key_terms.لِلْمَسَاكِينِ: designated for the poor and needy
key_terms.مَضْمُونًا: an offering whose liability is binding upon the person
key_terms.نَذْرًا: a vowed act made obligatory upon oneself
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial offering sent for hajj or sacred offering
key_terms.يَمِينٍ: a binding oath or sworn obligation

ai.seo_question: Can a person eat from a damaged sacrificial offering in hajj if it was obligatory or vowed?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the ruling on a sacrificial offering that becomes damaged. If the offering was obligatory due to a binding commitment such as a nadhr or a penalty, it must be replaced and one may not eat from it, as it is designated for the needy. If it was not obligatory, no replacement is required and one may eat from it.
